newsitem.title: CHINA: FORECAST-Chinese yuan to change little next month.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-Chinese yuan to change little next month.

text.p: The yuan is likely to move in a narrow range at around 8.2920 against the U.S. dollar in the next month despite upward pressure from an oversupply of dollars on the domestic market, analysts said on Sunday.

The surplus of dollars on the Shanghai-based China Foreign Exchange Trade System, an interbank market, would likely be offset by central bank intervention to curb the yuan's uptrend amid a growing trade surplus, they said.

Beijing said its trade surplus reached $13.92 billion in the first five months of 1997, compared with a trade deficit of $451 million in the same period last year. China chalked up a trade surplus of $10.29 billion in January-April.
The growing trade surplus has been a major factor supporting the yuan's gradual upward trend since the beginning of this year, analysts say.
China had a trade surplus of $12 billion for all of 1996 and analysts said they expected the figure to be much higher for 1997.
Analysts said traders had expected a slowdown in growth of the trade surplus figures and that the mounting surplus would put further upward pressure on the yuan.
"Market sentiment has been cautious in the past few days," one analyst said, adding that the yuan would likely stick to the 8.2920 level for the foreseeable future.
The People's Bank of China, the central bank, would likely intervene to keep the yuan down as it did on June 5 when the yuan approached the key 8.2900 resistance level, traders said.
"That action has cautioned traders that the stability of the yuan is still a top concern of the central government," said one trader.
"The intervention put strong psychological pressure on the market, making traders reluctant to push up the yuan despite a dollar oversupply," one local banker said.
"The central bank has been buying dollars on the market to prevent the yuan from rising sharply and to build up China's foreign exchange reserves," he added.
China said its foreign exchange reserves hit a record high $115 billion at the end of April against $105 billion at the end of last year.
Bankers said the surging reserves were mainly due to steady foreign investment inflows, China's strong trade surplus and the presence of more foreign financial institutions doing business in China.
Those factors had also contributed to the yuan's rise over the past few years, they said.
The yuan rose 0.3 percent against the dollar in 1996 after a rise of 2.9 percent in 1994 and 1.5 percent in 1995. It has been on a slight rising trend since the beginning of this year.
Industry sources said Beijing would buy more dollars whenever necessary to ensure the stability of the yuan in the run-up to July 1, when the British colony of Hong Kong reverts to Chinese rule.

"The central bank needs to consolidate its foreign exchange reserves at least in the short term, partly due to Hong Kong's return to China," said one banker. "It will not hesitate to buy dollars to depress the yuan on the interbank market."
